findings.antecedent: Animal social life (species-specific interaction distances, territoriality)
findings.consequent: "preprogrammed" behavior, instinctive attachment to place
findings.quote: Observations conducted on a wide variety of animals indicated species-specific interaction distances (Hediger 1964, 1968), which seemed to be 'preprogrammed.' Additionally, animal social life seemed to be regulated by territoriality, an instinctive attachment to place (Wynne-Edwards 1964; Eibl-Eibesfeldt 1970).

findings.antecedent: Situations disrupting personal and social spatial domains (crowding, territorial invasions) in animals
findings.consequent: Abnormal behavior, psychological stress (aggression, pathologies)
findings.quote: it was thought to be obvious that placing animals in situations that disrupt personal and social spatial domains would create abnormal behavior and psychological stress.

findings.antecedent: Very close individual distances, territorial invasions, or overcrowded conditions in humans
findings.consequent: Heightened arousal (measured by self-reports and machines)
findings.quote: Several studies in fact found a relationship between spatial circumstances and heightened arousal as measured by self-reports and machines (Aiello et al 1975; Baxter & Deanovitch 1970; McBride et al 1965; Smith & Haythorn 1972; Evans 1978).

findings.antecedent: Abnormal spatial situations (infringement of spatial domain) in humans
findings.consequent: Specific kinds of responses (e.g., aggression)
findings.quote: There is no consistent evidence, however, that abnormal spatial situations elicit specific kinds of responses among humans.

findings.consequent: Variation in appropriate interpersonal distances and densities
findings.quote: Hall... noted that persons from different cultures vary in the interpersonal distances and densities that they consider to be appropriate.

findings.consequent: Spatial behavior (interaction distance, density preference, touching)
findings.quote: 'Contact cultures' are considered to be highly involved in their interactions and thus use small interaction distances, like high densities, and engage in frequent touching... 'Noncontact cultures,' on the other hand, shun touching, dislike high densities, and avoid close interpersonal distances.

findings.consequent: Different spatial preferences
findings.quote: Further, Hall (1966:172–73) argued that even subcultures within the United States (e.g. blacks, Puerto Ricans, Northern Europeans) exhibit different spatial preferences.

findings.consequent: Spatial behavior (interaction distances)
findings.quote: The data on interpersonal distances support the notion that cultural differences do exist, although the methods used in these experiments have been less than ideal.

findings.antecedent: Teachers' actions (rewarding proper distance, punishing close approaches, prompting distant individuals)
findings.consequent: Children's personal distances
findings.quote: A more powerful factor seemed to be the teachers in these settings, who rewarded what they saw as proper interpersonal distance, punished children who approached others too closely, and physically prompted individuals who maintained distances too far from others (see also Bailey et al 1973).

findings.consequent: Adjustment of personal distances
findings.quote: The results of this study and others indicate that spatial behavior is no more a cultural trait than it is a biological instinct, since individuals adjust their personal distances on the basis of new contingencies.

findings.antecedent: Physical characteristics of a setting (buildings, microenvironment, design)
findings.consequent: Attitudes and actions
findings.quote: this view assumes that the physical characteristics of a setting per se have a large influence on our attitudes and actions, rather than our environments 'triggering' a biological or cultural trait.

findings.consequent: Healthy and happy tenants
findings.quote: The belief was that 'good' design can lead to healthy and happy tenants, while 'bad' design can have disastrous effects on residents.

findings.antecedent: Design factors (e.g., lack of territoriality, lack of community surveillance)
findings.consequent: Differential crime rates in urban public housing
findings.quote: One of the most widely publicized examples of the environmental perspective is the book Defensible Space (Newman 1973), which claimed that differential rates of crime in urban public housing could be explained by design factors.

findings.antecedent: Design forcing spatial proximity (low-rise, high-density, shared facilities)
findings.consequent: Social interaction, community spirit, cooperation, communality
findings.quote: Similar research indicates that design can force spatial proximity, and this inevitably leads to social interaction and community spirit.

findings.consequent: Social and psychological difficulties (rather than density per se)
findings.quote: There has also been a view expressed that it is environmental design that causes social and psychological difficulties and not density per se (Mitchell 1974).

findings.antecedent: Well-planned interior design (e.g., even distribution of objects/resources)
findings.consequent: Alleviation of crowding difficulties (e.g., clustering of people)
findings.quote: A well-planned interior design is thus seen as the solution to difficulties associated with crowding.

findings.consequent: Group formation and interaction
findings.quote: Osmond (1957, 1959) coined the terms 'sociopetal' and 'sociofu-gal' to suggest that interior design can encourage or discourage group formation.

findings.consequent: Pathology among the general population (rather than spatial factors)
findings.quote: An examination of the literature on the impact of crowding, for example, suggests that it is social structural factors and not spatial factors that cause pathology among the general population (see Cassel 1971; Fischer & Baldassare 1975).

findings.antecedent: Physical distances and high density per se
findings.consequent: Specific individual responses
findings.quote: Physical distances among individuals and high density per se were poor predictors of specific individual responses, and this led to a closer examination of social and psychological factors operating within settings.

findings.consequent: Poorer academic performance and health
findings.quote: Stokols et al (1977) found that perceived crowding was related to poorer academic performance and health among university students.

findings.consequent: Perceived household crowding
findings.quote: First, when examining survey items on perceived crowding, only a moderate amount of the vari-ance seems to be explained by objective household space (i.e. persons per room), which indicates that objective density is only part of the spatial problem in these homes.

findings.consequent: Housing satisfaction and preferred mobility
findings.quote: Second, perceived household crowding has an independent effect on measures of housing satisfaction (i.e. when account-ing for persons per room), including an impact on preferred mobility (see also Rossi 1955).

findings.consequent: Increased room density without adverse psychological effects (due to decreased visible social stimuli)
findings.quote: For example, in Desor's (1972) previously cited simulation, she found that subjects placed more figures within a space as the number of partitions increased. This indicated to her that room density may be increased (with no adverse psychological effects) when the number of visible social stimuli decrease.

findings.consequent: Faster pedestrian walking speed (suggesting minimization of social stimulation)
findings.quote: A study conducted by Bornstein & Bornstein (1976) found that pedestrians walked through the streets faster as city size increased, which suggested to the authors that the more crowded individuals were trying to minimize the level of social stimulation they experienced.

findings.consequent: Task and performance deficits
findings.quote: Yet another field experiment in a department store in New York City suggested that people had task and performance deficits due to overstimulation in dense shopping environments (Saegert et al 1975).

findings.consequent: Involvement in primary relationships (no withdrawal) and involvement in secondary social encounters (decrease)
findings.quote: The results of social survey analyses suggest that individuals experiencing residential crowding do not withdraw from primary relationships (friends, social networks, family, organizations), though they seem to decrease involvement in social encounters of a more secondary nature (reactions to strangers, neighboring, meeting new people), which indicates a cost-effective method of limiting social overload.

findings.consequent: Task deficits among children
findings.quote: A field study found that chronic household crowding created task deficits among children (Rodin 1976).

findings.consequent: Negative aspects of spatial shortages
findings.quote: Therefore, if people's perceptions of control are increased, the negative aspects of spatial shortages can be alleviated (Sherrod & Cohen 1977).

findings.antecedent: Low social status and high demand for space
findings.consequent: Less claim to space
findings.quote: This readily brings to mind the fact that people of low status (e.g. the urban poor, the child in the crowded household) may have less of a claim to space when it is in high demand than do people of high status (the urban affluent, adults in the home).

findings.antecedent: Actual power over spatial use (more vs. less)
findings.consequent: Overload and interference (decrease with more power), interruptions and inability to conduct preferred activities (increase with less power)
findings.quote: Actual power over spatial use should minimize overload and allow one to conduct desired activities with less interference, while less power would lead to more interruptions and the inability to conduct preferred activities.

findings.antecedent: Interaction between low social power, attitude of powerlessness, and crowding
findings.consequent: Generalized learned helplessness among low-income crowded children
findings.quote: In fact, it is this subgroup (i.e. low in real and felt power) that may actually be the basis of Rodin's (1976) findings of a generalized learned helplessness among low-income crowded children.

findings.antecedent: Stable, status-differentiated group experiencing a shortage of space
findings.consequent: Greater control over space use and activities (e.g., scheduling, regulating utilization)
findings.quote: A common response of a stable, status-differentiated group experi-encing a shortage of space is greater control over space use and activities in its territory.

findings.antecedent: People's imagery of spaces (fantasy vs. reality)
findings.consequent: Coping with existing circumstances and imagining better positions
findings.quote: Sometimes the images people have of their spaces are more fantasy than reality, and Lym (1978a,b) argues that people develop these images in order to cope with the existing circumstances and imagine themselves in better positions.

findings.consequent: Spatial differentiation and mechanisms for controlling movement across boundaries (privacy)
findings.quote: In other words, role differentiation demands some degree of spatial differentiation within territories (Lym 1978b) and a mechanism for controlling movement across boundaries.

findings.antecedent: Disagreement on space allocation for role enactments
findings.consequent: Interpersonal tension and role interference
findings.quote: Problems arise when those sharing a common space do not have the same views about how this resource should be allocated, since this could hinder the enactment of individually preferred roles.

findings.antecedent: Short supply of household space (lack of room/privacy)
findings.consequent: Role conflict, competition for space, incomplete role performances, intrusions, blocking of desired role enactments, loss of control over boundary mechanisms
findings.quote: If there is not enough room or privacy to conduct desired roles alone and with others, competition for space use may occur. Undoubtedly, the possibilities of incomplete role performances, intrusions, and the blocking of desired role enactments are heightened.

findings.antecedent: Alteration of one nonverbal factor (e.g., distance)
findings.consequent: Shifts in another nonverbal factor (e.g., eye contact) to maintain optimal interaction
findings.quote: Importantly, the alteration of one factor seemed to create shifts along another dimension (e.g. closer distances led to less eye contact, or vice versa). Thus, they argued for an 'optimal' distance when, not attained, led to compensatory reactions to decrease the stress felt from the inappropriateness of the situation.

findings.consequent: Optimal distances for interaction; comfort and distance relationship is not always monotonic
findings.quote: Another reexamination of the research literature by Sundstrom & Altman (1976) supports the basic premise that there are optimal distances for interactions varying in level of involvement (interacting friends and strangers; non-interacting strangers), suggests that the relationship between comfort and distance need not be monotonic in every case (e.g. close and far distances are not desired for most interactions), and argues that other compensations are available when spatial variables are unadjustable.

findings.consequent: Objective value (resource) and communicative roles in social life
findings.quote: Space obviously has value for individuals and should be consid-ered as a resource, as is time or money. It is cherished by some, denied to others, and competed for by all.

findings.antecedent: Spatial behavior and uses, environmental cues, and positions others take in space
findings.consequent: Information about expectations and relationships
findings.quote: Beyond its objective value, spatial behavior and uses have communicative roles in social life. Reactions to our use of space, environmental cues, and the positions others take in space all inform us of what is expected of us and how others relate to our presence.
